# For the Win — selected additions from the November digest

The creator supplied a refreshed Bookworm digest on 2026-11-12. It attributes
its account to Kevin Werbach and Dan Hunter's For the Win, in the Russian
translation by A. Kardash (2015). The reviewed note revision has SHA-256
3930ec52fbef77fe1a79b6a431c10bbf07b4767cc24e23d6ba03aa252871e23f.
Section IDs below refer to that private digest's indexed snapshot. This
paraphrase preserves selected design reasoning and historical examples from
the digest. The cases illustrate possible mechanisms without establishing
effect sizes, causality or current product facts.

sections.title: Suitability depends on the activity
sections.text:
## Suitability depends on the activity

Compare four questions for each proposed activity: whose motivation needs
support, what meaningful choice exists, whether the desired behavior and its
quality can be observed, and what current incentives could conflict. The
digest's supermarket example contrasts easily measured checkout speed with
limited worker choice and a customer loyalty program that may give customers
some discretion about rewards. The second still needs a worthwhile goal.
Rank the desired outcomes and remove proposed mechanisms from the goal list.
A leaderboard describes a means. Useful, accurate contributions could be
an outcome. Map each proposed scored action to that outcome and its quality
check. Sources in the digest: R003, R006, R010–R013 and R024–R025.

sections.title: Feedback can inform or pressure
sections.text:
## Feedback can inform or pressure

An external purpose can become personally endorsed. Studying statistics for
a chosen profession is a different reason for doing the same activity from
studying to avoid punishment. With an already interesting activity, an
expected reward for meeting a quota can direct attention toward the cheapest
way to earn it. Unexpected recognition or feedback that explains progress can
have a different meaning. For a routine task, an external cue may help someone
get started. Inspect what the feedback measures, how it will be used and
what choice people have. Sources in the digest: R014–R017 and R029.

sections.title: The same component can support different mechanics
sections.text:
## The same component can support different mechanics

A team can organize mutual help on a shared task or organize competition
between teams. The dynamic of belonging depends on the resulting
relationships. Compare personal milestones, groups with a meaningful
reference point, and collective goals according to the intended outcome.
A score that people can spend or trade creates additional incentives to
accumulate and exchange it. A progress indicator can simply communicate
how far a person has come. Sources in the digest: R019–R024, R031 and R034.

sections.title: Match the two timescales to the participant's experience
sections.text:
## Match the two timescales to the participant's experience

In the short loop the response to one action changes the motivation for the
next. Across sessions, a newcomer may need a first achievable task and an
experienced participant may need a harder challenge, a chance to consolidate
a skill, or a new role. The book's Lift example describes trading complex
habit mechanics for simple encouragement and feedback from personal history.
Observe how people use the revised mechanism. More immediate use, competence
and sustained voluntary use are distinct outcomes. Sources in the digest:
R014, R024, R026–R027, R033 and R034.

sections.title: Follow the incentives outside the score
sections.text:
## Follow the incentives outside the score

The book describes workers skipping breaks under a speed ranking. Consider
who sees the ranking, whether it affects evaluation and what declining
participation costs. In its Lloyds example, an exchangeable currency created
inflation while conversations between investors and authors helped develop
ideas. Evaluate the side effects separately. If collaboration is the goal,
preserve useful conversations and address the currency problem. If fair
selection through prices is the goal, examine whether those conversations
undermine that outcome. The Seriosity example illustrates a further failure:
the price of sending a message outweighed the benefit perceived by senders.
Track participation and the quality or real benefit it was intended to
produce separately. The digest's legal topics are historical prompts to
identify applicable questions. Sources in the digest: R006, R024 and R028–R034.
